newsitem.title: UK: Oil traders see Iraq export lull if UN deal renewe.
newsitem.headline: Oil traders see Iraq export lull if UN deal renewe.

text.p: Even if the United Nations decides to extend the oil-for-food agreement with Iraq, world oil markets can expect a lull in Iraqi crude exports of about a month, oil traders said on Tuesday.

U.N. officials will decide soon whether to renew the current six month agreement which ends on June 7. The accord allows Iraq to sell up to $2 billion of oil to purchase food, medicine and other goods.
But if a rollover is agreed the bureaucracy involved in the signing of new export contracts is likely to stall fresh crude sales until late June, traders said.

"Nothing will load before later in June, not before the paper work has been done and contracts have been given approval...and applications from any newcomers have been sorted out," said one European lifter of Iraqi oil.
Exports under the first six-month period are already tailing off.
The final loading of two million barrels of Kirkuk crude at the Turkish port of Ceyhan was scheduled for last Sunday, two weeks ahead of the contract expiry.

Meanwhile, traders speculated that two cargoes of Basrah Light due to load at the Gulf port of Mina al-Bakr in the final two weeks of the programme could be cancelled to prevent Iraqi revenues nudging over the $2 billion limit.
Exports from both terminals have been running at about 750,000 barrels per day (bpd) in recent weeks.
"Things are drying up now and we're definitely going to be seeing a bit of a hiatus before we see the next lot of barrels," a trader said.
The lull should result in a tightening of high sulphur, or sour crude markets which over the past few months have had been depressed by increasing flows of Iraqi crude.
Russian Urals, Europe's benchmark sour crude, slipped from around Dated Brent minus 80 cents in mid January to a low of Dated Brent minus $1.43 late last week.
Iraqi crude buyers on Tuesday said they were optimistic that the oil-for-food deal would be extended.
Last week, Yasushi Akashi, U.N. undersecretary-general for humanitarian affairs said that a rollover of the oil-for-food deal was a "foregone conclusion".

But doubt remained over the enthusiasm of the United States. On Saturday U.S ambassador to the U.N. Bill Richardson said the Clinton administration was reserving judgement on whether the agreement should be extended.
"We're very optimistic but still waiting for the green light," said an Italian refiner.
Traders said they were already sending letters of intent via telex to Iraq's State Oil Marketing Organisation (SOMO) to seek contracts under a renewed U.N. deal.
